snippet.textDisplay: Hi Dr. Sinclair! Thank you for posting this video as I am a new subscriber to your channel. My mom has signs of early dementia and this is all very new to me as an adult and caregiver. I am trying to educate my father as he is her main caregiver with your video and channel. I feel this topic is not discussed enough when it comes to aging and I’m glad you are using this platform to share your knowledge of how to take care of dementia family members. Your explanation of defensive behavior and anxiety is so  on point as that is the main signs of my moms behavior besides being forgetful. She gets overwhelmed and agitated quickly. I always try to diffuse the situation and help her especially when she forgets why she went to the kitchen to do something. What amazes me is she knows every word of songs she grew up with! She is a 50s baby and she still remembers music which makes me so happy as I find music to be very therapeutic. Anyways I wish I could give you a hug through the screen as this is not an easy thing to navigate as her daughter. Thank you again for creating your channel and these wonderful educational videos. 💜✨

snippet.textDisplay: Dr. Sinclair: thank you for your calm explanations and suggestions. I wish I had heard your recommendations back when I was caring for my mother. I had been mentally prepared to deal with an aging parent with physical limitations, but I never anticipated the mental decline since my mother had been so sharp until very late in life. It turns out that caring for someone with dementia is 1,000 times worse than anything I had ever experienced while caring for sick/elderly grandparents. It wasn't only the loss of memories--which was bad enough--it was having to deal with a change in my mother's personality too. My funny and jovial mother became angry, combative, suspicious, and in the very end, she became terrified of the idea of being abandoned and needed someone to be next to her at all times. I was losing my mother before she was actually gone and I couldn't rely on logic to soothe her fears or clarify her misconceptions, etc. I realize now that I felt so much anger and frustration because I was battling to accept our new reality.

snippet.textDisplay:
Anna, thank you for putting into words what so many care partners experience but struggle to articulate. The ambiguous loss and anticipatory grief that come with dementia are incredibly heavy to carry. As you described so beautifully, it’s not only the loss of memories - it’s the shift in personality and the realization that logic no longer reaches the person you once knew so well.

What you shared about the anger and frustration that can arise while trying to accept this new reality is something many caregivers quietly wrestle with. There is so much grief in that space.

Thank you for taking the time to share your experience and wisdom here. I have no doubt your words will resonate with - and help - many others in this community. ❤️

snippet.textDisplay:
Dealing with my MIL with dementia. I used to visit her once or twice a week for a coffee. We used to chat, gossip, laugh. Now - I don’t know how to talk with her. She complains incessantly about false realities. I would try to explain - but that doesn’t work. I try to just empathize, but that doesn’t help her anxiety about the false reality. I try to change the subject to something more positive, but then she will have an incorrect negative perception to that positive topic.

Not only has she lost her memory, it’s been replaced by a completely different reality.

The people (neighbors and church friends) that used to visit her do not visit anymore because no one can talk with her.

snippet.textDisplay: short-term memory loss has always been a joke between my best friend and I. Her physician told her years ago, that if you forget where your keys are, that's s.t. memory loss, not to be worried about; if you forget what your keys are FOR, that's a whole nother thing. I've always leaned on that distinction. Last month I was dx'd with early dementia, Alzheimer's variety. I'm not going to stick around if/when I get to the "what are these keys for?" stage. Have told my physician this, and bless the man, he understands and has referred me to one of the only two docs locally who delivers MAID--just for discussion at this point--but it's SO good to know I don't have to stick around as I diminish more and more and more.

snippet.textDisplay:
My Loved one does this to!
So… I hang onto the stuff which I do not want/ it’s clutter. How do YOU manage this?
snippet.textOriginal:
My Loved one does this to! 
So… I hang onto the stuff which I do not want/ it’s clutter. How do YOU manage this?

snippet.textDisplay:
Bee, thank you for sharing, this is such a common challenge for many of my carepartners.
For many people with dementia, holding onto items becomes a way to feel safe and reduce anxiety, even when the clutter feels overwhelming to you.

A few gentle strategies that often help:

• Use forced choices:
“Hey, we need to clear a few things—would you like to keep this or that?”
This preserves a sense of control without overwhelming them.

• Do major decluttering when they’re out of the house, if possible.
If they later ask about an item, you can say something like:
“Oh, I cleaned up earlier. I can’t remember where I put it right now, but I’ll help you look after I finish dinner,”
and then calmly redirect.

The key is how and when you redirect...too fast can increase anxiety and feel dismissive, too slow can escalate distress. There really is an art to this so I’ll add this to my topic list and make a more in-depth video walking through it step by step. Hope that helps!
